blocks.text: How much GPU is needed is one of the most common practical questions in fine-tuning, and the honest answer is that it depends on model size, precision, and fine-tuning method, this topic pulls together the estimation approach from concepts covered across earlier modules into a single practical reference.
Rather than memorizing fixed numbers, understanding the components that make up total memory use, covered below, lets you estimate GPU requirements for any specific model and method combination.
1. The Core Factors That Determine GPU Need

blocks.alt: Model parameter count, precision choice, and fine-tuning method combine into an estimated GPU memory need

blocks.text: Three factors dominate the GPU memory estimate, how many parameters the model has, what precision those parameters and training computations use, covered in the earlier Quantization module, and which fine-tuning method, full fine-tuning versus LoRA or QLoRA, both covered in earlier modules, is being used.
2. What Actually Consumes GPU Memory

blocks.alt: Model weights, optimizer states, gradients, and activations all consume GPU memory

blocks.text: Total training memory breaks down into model weights themselves, optimizer states, which for Adam-family optimizers, covered in an earlier module, can be larger than the weights themselves, gradients computed during the backward pass, and activations stored for that backward pass, each of these components scales differently depending on the method chosen.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Component","Rough Scaling"],"rows":[["Model weights","Proportional to parameter count and precision"],["Optimizer states","Often 2x model weights for full fine-tuning with Adam"],["Gradients","Proportional to trainable parameter count"],["Activations","Scales with batch size and sequence length"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Full Fine-Tuning vs QLoRA on a Large Model

blocks.alt: Full fine-tuning a 70B model needs very high memory while QLoRA needs dramatically less

blocks.text: This difference is stark at large model sizes, full fine-tuning a 70 billion parameter model, covered generally in the earlier Fine-Tune a 70B Model topic, needs the full optimizer state and gradient memory for every one of those parameters, QLoRA, covered in an earlier module, needs gradients and optimizer states only for the small LoRA adapter parameters, plus a quantized, frozen copy of the base weights, a dramatically smaller total.
4. Precision Directly Scales Weight Memory

blocks.alt: FP16 uses 2 bytes per parameter while 4-bit quantization uses 0.5 bytes per parameter

blocks.text: Weight memory scales directly and predictably with precision, a parameter stored in FP16 takes 2 bytes, the same parameter quantized to 4-bit, covered in the earlier Quantization module, takes roughly a quarter of that, this single factor alone can be the difference between a model fitting on one GPU or needing several.

code.content:
# Rough weight memory estimate
def estimate_weight_memory_gb(num_params_billions, bytes_per_param):
    return num_params_billions * bytes_per_param

# 7B model in FP16
print(estimate_weight_memory_gb(7, 2))   # roughly 14 GB
# 7B model in 4-bit
print(estimate_weight_memory_gb(7, 0.5)) # roughly 3.5 GB

blocks.text: 5. Single GPU vs Multi-GPU Thresholds

blocks.alt: Fitting on one GPU is compared against needing multiple GPUs

blocks.text: Once total estimated memory exceeds what a single available GPU provides, the distributed training techniques covered in an earlier module, tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, or DeepSpeed ZeRO stages, become necessary, understanding this threshold for a specific model and GPU combination is a core part of planning a fine-tuning project.
6. Rough Estimates vs Actual Profiling

blocks.alt: A rough back of envelope estimate is refined through actual memory profiling into a confirmed requirement

blocks.text: Back-of-envelope estimates like the ones covered in this topic are useful for initial planning, but actual memory use depends on implementation details, specific framework overhead, activation checkpointing settings, covered in an earlier module, and other factors, running an actual short training step and profiling real memory use confirms whether an estimate holds before committing to a full training run.

blocks.title: Always validate an estimate before committing significant compute budget
blocks.content: A rough estimate that is off by even twenty or thirty percent can mean the difference between a training run comfortably fitting and one that fails partway through with an out-of-memory error, a quick profiling run is cheap insurance against that outcome.

blocks.text: 7. Batch Size Effect on Memory

blocks.alt: A larger batch size requires more activation memory

blocks.text: Beyond the model itself, batch size directly affects activation memory, a larger batch size processes more examples in parallel per step, needing proportionally more memory for the activations stored during the forward pass, gradient accumulation, covered in an earlier module, offers a way to get the effective benefit of a larger batch size without the full memory cost.
8. A Practical Estimation Workflow

A practical approach starts with the rough weight memory calculation covered above, adds an estimate for optimizer states and gradients based on the chosen method, full versus LoRA versus QLoRA, adds a buffer for activations based on expected batch size and sequence length, and then validates that total against actual available GPU memory before committing to a specific hardware plan.
9. How to Answer This in an Interview Setting

A strong answer to this question does not recite a single fixed number, it walks through the factors covered in this topic, parameter count, precision, and method, and shows how to derive an estimate for a specific scenario, demonstrating understanding of what actually drives GPU memory use rather than memorized figures.
Worked Example

Asked how much GPU memory a 13 billion parameter model needs for QLoRA fine-tuning, a strong answer estimates the quantized 4-bit base weights at roughly 6.5 GB, adds a modest amount for the small trainable LoRA adapter parameters and their optimizer states, and adds a buffer for activations that scales with batch size and sequence length, arriving at a total that comfortably fits on a single mid-range GPU, a dramatically different answer than the same model would need for full fine-tuning.
The candidate then notes they would confirm this estimate with an actual short profiling run before committing to a full training plan, following the validation approach covered in this topic.
Common Mistakes

items: Reciting a memorized GPU memory number without explaining the underlying factors that actually determine it
Forgetting that optimizer states, not just model weights, are often the largest memory component for full fine-tuning
Not accounting for activation memory scaling with batch size and sequence length when estimating total requirements
Committing to a full training run based purely on a rough estimate without a quick profiling validation step first

blocks.text: Practice

For a specific model size you choose, walk through the estimation workflow covered in this topic to estimate GPU memory needs for both full fine-tuning and QLoRA, and identify at what point, if any, the full fine-tuning estimate would require the distributed training techniques covered in an earlier module.
Key Takeaway

GPU memory requirements for fine-tuning depend on model parameter count, precision, and fine-tuning method, breaking down into weight memory, optimizer state memory, gradient memory, and activation memory, and while rough estimates from these factors are useful for planning, actual profiling should always confirm the estimate before committing significant compute budget to a full training run.
